metadata.title: School performance and inequality of opportunities in Latin America

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 10 Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Panama, Peru, Uruguay) and applies OECD guidance for plausible-score estimation by taking into account all ten plausible score values and the 80 PISA replicates. The methodology section describes a multilevel educational production function approach (students nested in schools) rather than reporting explicit use of student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight variables by name. Because the paper does not state a specific complex-survey weight variable, the safest interpretation is that weighting is handled through the OECD plausible-values/replicate framework rather than via explicitly named sampling weights. Missing values are replaced with each variable’s country average, which is a preprocessing step applied before estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2018 dataset for students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months in the 10 participating Latin American countries. The analysis estimates a multilevel educational production function with students nested in schools, using the full available sample for these countries as described (75,622 students across schools). Missing values for each variable were replaced by the country’s average value of the respective variable. For achievement outcomes, the study incorporates all ten PISA plausible score values and the 80 PISA replicates (OECD 2009) when estimating the models.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel model coefficients (no ML metrics reported). Key estimates: Gender 9.406 (SE 0.639, p<0.001); Age 12.115 (SE 0.956, p<0.001); Preschool 4.517 (SE 0.698, p<0.001); Repetition −49.290 (SE 0.745, p<0.001); Insecurity −1.026 (SE 0.675, not significant); Teacher feedback not estimated for Reading (shown as '–' in Table 4); Family background 7.312 (SE 0.300, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading achievement the study leveraged grade repetition, gender, preschool attendance, and family background index (plus other student and school inputs) to explain reading performance, finding that grade repetition is strongly negatively associated with reading while family background and age are positively associated. This indicates that reducing grade repetition and addressing socioeconomic barriers through family- and school-support policies may improve reading outcomes, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel model coefficients (no ML metrics reported). Key estimates: Gender −18.451 (SE 0.642, p<0.001); Age 10.564 (SE 1.039, p<0.001); Preschool 6.731 (SE 0.878, p<0.001); Repetition −44.848 (SE 1.061, p<0.001); Feedback from teachers perceived by the student −3.014 (SE 0.341, p<0.001); Family background 8.148 (SE 0.439, p<0.001); Medium city 623.594 (SE 70.932, p<0.001); Large city 1749.315 (SE 103.410, p<0.001); No. computer 2788.170 (SE 1158.410, p<0.01); Creative extracurricular activities 60.378 (SE 21.907, p<0.001); Adaptation of instruction 23.013 (SE 5.932, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics achievement the study leveraged grade repetition, gender, preschool attendance, family background index, and teacher feedback (student-perceived) to explain mathematics performance, finding that grade repetition and perceived teacher feedback are strongly negatively associated with achievement while family background and instructional adaptation are positively associated. This indicates that equity-oriented policies should prioritize preventing grade repetition and improving how teachers deliver feedback and adapt instruction, though causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional multilevel associations.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel model coefficients (no ML metrics reported). Key estimates: Gender −12.052 (SE 0.593, p<0.001); Age 11.518 (SE 1.075, p<0.001); Preschool 4.226 (SE 0.838, p<0.001); Repetition −43.933 (SE 0.726, p<0.001); Feedback from teachers perceived by the student −3.198 (SE 0.346, p<0.001); Family background 7.053 (SE 0.395, p<0.001); Creative extracurricular activities 1717.215 (SE 106.879, p<0.01); Adaptation of instruction not significant/absent in Table 4 (shown as '–'); Teacher behavior hindering learning 56.792 (SE 22.867, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science achievement the study leveraged grade repetition, gender, preschool attendance, family background index, and teacher behavior hindering learning to explain science performance, finding that grade repetition and perceived teacher feedback are strongly negatively associated with achievement while family background is positively associated and teacher behavior hindering learning is negatively related to science outcomes. This indicates that science improvement efforts should combine early support (e.g., preschool and retention prevention) with classroom practice reforms that reduce harmful teacher behaviors, while recognizing that the study’s design does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 student achievement in Latin America (10 countries: ARG, BRA, CHL, COL, CRI, DOM, MEX, PAN, PER, URY) using a multilevel educational production function framework with students nested in schools. Outcomes are PISA standardized reading, mathematics, and science scores, estimated using all ten plausible values and the 80 PISA replicates, with missing values replaced by each variable’s country average. The reported results are multilevel regression coefficients rather than ML predictive metrics: grade repetition shows large negative associations across all three domains, while family background is consistently positive. In mathematics and science, student-perceived teacher feedback is significantly negative, and instructional adaptation is positive for mathematics. The paper is cross-sectional, so findings describe associations and heterogeneity by socioeconomic context rather than causal impacts.
